front.text: Emotions are high. Reaction is tempting. How you show up will often shape the outcome more than your words.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Pause before responding or deciding anything
• Name the emotion internally, not externally
• Choose timing and setting intentionally

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: What outcome do I want from this conversation?
Strong emotions push leaders to act before they’re ready.

front.text: You don’t have the title. Influence matters most here. Authority won't carry this conversation, trust and credibility will.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Lead with credibility, not positional control
• Ask before directing
• Build alignment before expecting compliance

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: What does this person care about most and how can I influence them?
Influence grows faster than authority.

title: Leading Someone More Experienced Than You

front.text: They bring deep experience. Their perspective matters. You don’t have to know more than them to have this conversation.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Lead with curiosity, not comparison
• Invite experience as an asset, not a threat
• Leverage their insights for the benefit of the team

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Am I respecting their experience and insights?
Humility and curiosity lay a foundation of trust and respect.

front.text: Performance is below the standard. The issue isn’t fixing itself. Pressure feels tempting here, but clarity usually works better.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Slow down before applying pressure or consequences
• Separate clarity issues from accountability issues
• Diagnose effort, energy, and expectations before correcting behavior

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Is this a clarity problem, a capability problem, or a commitment problem?
Low performance requires clarity before pressure.

title: Leading a High Performer with a Bad Attitude

front.text: Results are strong. Behavior is costly. Others notice. Their results are buying them more room than they should have.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Separate performance from behavior
• Address impact without excusing results
• Reinforce standards consistently

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: What behavior am I tolerating because the results are strong?
Performance never excuses behavior.

title: Leading Someone Who Doesn’t Respect You

front.text: Pushback is constant. Tone feels dismissive. Boundaries are tested. This isn’t about the conversation, it's about credibility.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Stay grounded instead of defensive
• Address behavior directly, not emotionally
• Reinforce expectations through consistency

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Am I trying to force respect or earn it?
Respect follows clarity, not force.

front.text: The relationship has changed. Expectations feel awkward. Roles are unclear. You stepped into a new role, but never reset the relationship.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Acknowledge the shift openly - don’t pretend nothing changed
• Set new expectations early: role, decision rights, standards
• Avoid overcorrecting or overcompensating to “prove” authority

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Am I avoiding clarity to protect the relationship, or creating clarity to protect the team?
Role changes create confusion. Leaders offer clarity.

front.text: Power dynamics are real. Stakes feel higher. Silence feels safer. You're trying to help, but how this sounds matters more than what you say.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Lead with alignment around outcomes, not position
• Clarify expectations, priorities, and constraints
• Frame concerns around outcomes, not opinions

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Am I trying to be right, or trying to be effective?
Upward leadership requires clarity and trust.

front.text: They want to do well. Standards aren’t clear yet. Habits are forming. What you reinforce now becomes the baseline.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Be explicit instead of assuming understanding
• Reinforce standards early, before habits set in
• Normalize questions and feedback from day one

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: What behaviors am I unintentionally allowing to become the standard?
Early clarity prevents difficult conversations later.

front.text: Deadlines are tight. Stress is high. Speed feels urgent. When everything feels urgent, prioritization quietly disappears.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Slow your thinking even if action must be fast
• Prioritize clarity over speed
• Set the tone with calm and steady behavior

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: What needs clarity right now before anything else moves?
You set the temperature for your team.

front.text: Others are watching. Timing matters. Impact is amplified. Whatever you do here teaches more than you intend.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Protect dignity publicly
• Address specifics privately
• Be intentional about audience and timing

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Am I trying to correct behavior, or protect trust in this moment?
Public moments shape trust quickly.

front.text: Past issues linger. Intent is questioned. Progress feels fragile. This conversation won’t rebuild trust. What you do after it will.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Slow the pace before pushing forward
• Address what broke trust directly
• Stay consistent and rebuild trust before expecting change

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Am I acknowledging and addressing the trust issue or ignoring it and hoping it goes away?
Trust must be rebuilt before performance improves.

front.text: Side conversations spread. Trust erodes quietly. Energy drops. Silence here looks like permission.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Address behavior early and directly
• Reinforce standards consistently - in public and private
• Redirect negative conversations toward solutions

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Am I allowing side conversations to replace direct ones?
What goes unaddressed becomes normal.

front.text: Small misses accumulate. Tolerance increases. Expectations blur. What used to be “not okay” is starting to feel normal.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Re-anchor expectations clearly
• Enforce standards consistently
• Address drift before it becomes the standard

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: What have I been letting slide that I need to address this week?
What's tolerated becomes what’s expected.

title: Leading After You’ve Let Things Slide

front.text: No accountability. A reset is necessary. Time has made addressing it extremely uncomfortable. It feels awkward because you waited, not because you're wrong.
Adjust before you act.

back.heading: Leader adjustment
back.text:
• Own the accountability gap without defensiveness
• Reset expectations explicitly
• Follow through consistently

back.heading: Ask yourself
back.text: Am I prepared to fully commit to the reset and the necessary follow-through?
Credibility comes back through consistency.
